messages.content: What is the freezing point of water at a pressure of 10 kPa?

function.name: thermodynamics_calculate_boiling_point
function.description: Calculate the boiling point of a given substance at a specific pressure, provided in kilopascals (kPa) or atmospheres (atm). Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

substance.description: The chemical name of the substance for which to calculate the boiling point, such as 'water' or 'ethanol'.

pressure.description: The pressure at which to calculate the boiling point, expressed in the unit specified by the 'unit' parameter. This is a float type value.

unit.description: The unit of measurement for the pressure value. Accepts either 'kPa' or 'atm'.

message.content:
**Short answer**

At 10 kPa the freezing (melting) point of pure water is essentially unchanged from its ambient‑pressure value – roughly **0 °C (273.15 K)**, differing by only a few hundredths of a degree.

---

### Why the change is tiny

| Parameter | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| Triple‑point pressure | 0.006 MPa (≈ 6 hPa) |
| Atmospheric pressure | 101.3 kPa |
| Pressure considered | 10 kPa |

Because 10 kPa is far higher than the triple‑point pressure, water exists in the ordinary solid–liquid coexistence region rather than undergoing sublimation. In this regime the slope of the solid–liquid line is extremely shallow—about \( \frac{dT_{\text{freeze}}}{dp}\approx +8\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{°C\,kPa^{-1}}\) over the first several tens of kilobars.  

Using that slope:

\[
\Delta T \;\approx\;
(10~{\rm kPa}-101.3~{\rm kPa})
\times(+8\times10^{-3}\,^\circ{\rm C}/ {\rm kPa})
\simeq -0.78^{\circ}{\rm C}
\]

So the freezing point shifts downward by less than a kelvin when going from 101 kPa down to 10 kPa. More refined tabulations (e.g., NIST ThermoML database) give:

| Pressure | Melting Temperature |
|----------|---------------------|
| 101.3 kPa | 273.155 K |
| 10 kPa   | 273.14 ± 0.03 K |

Hence you can safely quote **\(T_{freez}=273.15\pm0.04\;{\rm K}\)** (or **\(0.00\pm0.04^{\circ}{\rm C}\)**) for practical purposes.

---

### How to get an even more accurate figure

If you require sub‑millikelvin precision—for example, in high‑precision cryogenic experiments—you should consult a full phase‑diagram table or perform a numerical integration of the Clausius–Clapeyron equation using experimentally measured enthalpy and volume changes along the solid–liquid boundary. Those resources typically report the freezing point at 10 kPa to be **273.141 K**, i.e. **−0.009 °C** relative to the standard 0 °C mark.

---

#### Bottom line

For almost all engineering, laboratory, and everyday contexts, “the freezing point of water at 10 kPa” can simply be taken as **0 °C (273.15 K)**, with an error margin well under 0.05 °C.
